section.title: Paul's Defense before the Crowd
section.sectionRationale: From the barracks steps Paul tells his story to the hostile crowd: a zealous Pharisee turned persecutor, arrested by the risen Jesus on the Damascus road, commissioned to be a witness, and finally sent far away to the Gentiles. That last word ignites fresh fury, but Paul's Roman citizenship halts a flogging, and the commander convenes the Sanhedrin to learn the charge.
section.thesis: Paul defends himself not by argument but by testimony, recounting how the risen Christ met him, cleansed him, and sent him to the Gentiles, so that his very conversion becomes the sermon, and the mention of the nations that so enrages the crowd reveals the heart of the gospel's reach.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the appeal for a hearing; the zealous persecutor's past; the risen Christ on the road; Ananias and the commission; the sending to the Gentiles that provokes the mob; and the citizen who cannot lawfully be flogged.

units.label: Brothers and fathers, my defense
units.note: a zealous persecutor of the Way

verses.text: “Brothers and fathers, listen now to my {{apologia|defense}} before you.”
When they heard him speak to them in Hebrew, they became even more silent. Then Paul declared,

“I am a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia, but raised in this city. I was educated at the feet of Gamaliel in strict conformity to the law of our fathers. I was just as zealous for God as any of you are today.
I persecuted this {{hodos|Way}} even to the death, detaining both men and women and throwing them into prison,

as the high priest and the whole Council can testify about me. I even obtained letters from them to their brothers in Damascus, and I was on my way to apprehend these people and bring them to Jerusalem to be punished.

units.label: The risen Christ on the road

verses.text: About noon as I was approaching Damascus, suddenly a bright light from heaven flashed around me.
I fell to the ground and heard a voice say to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?’
‘Who are You, Lord?’ I asked. ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting,’ He replied.
My companions saw the light, but they could not understand the voice of the One speaking to me.
Then I asked, ‘What should I do, Lord?’ ‘Get up and go into Damascus,’ He told me. ‘There you will be told all that you have been appointed to do.’
Because the brilliance of the light had blinded me, my companions led me by the hand into Damascus.

units.label: Ananias and the commission
units.note: to see the Righteous One and be His witness

verses.text: There a man named Ananias, a devout observer of the law who was highly regarded by all the Jews living there,
came and stood beside me. ‘Brother Saul,’ he said, ‘receive your sight.’ And at that moment I could see him.
Then he said, ‘The God of our fathers has appointed you to know His will and to see the {{dikaios|Righteous One}} and to hear His voice.
You will be His {{martys|witness}} to everyone of what you have seen and heard.
And now what are you waiting for? Get up, be baptized, and wash your sins away, calling on His name.’

units.label: Sent far away to the Gentiles
units.note: the word that ignites the crowd

verses.text: Later, when I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying at the temple, I fell into a trance
and saw the Lord saying to me, ‘Hurry! Leave Jerusalem quickly, because the people here will not accept your testimony about Me.’
‘Lord,’ I answered, ‘they know very well that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in You.
And when the blood of Your witness Stephen was shed, I stood there giving my approval and watching over the garments of those who killed him.’
Then He said to me, ‘Go! I will send you far away to the Gentiles.’”

units.label: Paul the Roman citizen
units.note: you cannot lawfully flog a citizen

verses.text: The crowd listened to Paul until he made this statement. Then they lifted up their voices and shouted, “Rid the earth of him! He is not fit to live!”
As they were shouting and throwing off their cloaks and tossing dust into the air,
the commander ordered that Paul be brought into the barracks. He directed that Paul be flogged and interrogated to determine the reason for this outcry against him.
But as they stretched him out to strap him down, Paul said to the centurion standing there, “Is it lawful for you to flog a Roman citizen without a trial?”
On hearing this, the centurion went and reported it to the commander. “What are you going to do?” he said. “This man is a Roman citizen.”
The commander went to Paul and asked, “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?” “Yes,” he answered.
“I paid a high price for my citizenship,” said the commander. “But I was born a citizen,” Paul replied.
At once those who were about to interrogate Paul stepped back, and the commander himself was alarmed when he realized that he had put a Roman citizen in chains.

The next day the commander, wanting to learn the real reason Paul was accused by the Jews, released him and ordered the chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin to assemble. Then he brought Paul down and had him stand before them.

apologia.gloss: A defense, a reasoned answer given in reply, the word behind apologetics. Paul offers not a legal plea but his testimony; his best defense of the gospel is the story of how the risen Christ met and changed him.

hodos.gloss: Way, road, path; an early name for the Christian movement, the Way. Paul once persecuted the Way to the death; now he belongs to it, proof that the road he tried to destroy is the road of the risen Lord.

dikaios.gloss: Righteous, just; the Righteous One is a title for the Messiah, Jesus. Ananias tells Paul that God appointed him to see the Righteous One, the same title used of Jesus at His trial and in Stephen's speech.

martys.gloss: Witness; the root of the word martyr. Paul is appointed a witness of the risen Christ to everyone, and the same word marks Stephen, whose blood Paul once approved, showing how a persecutor became a witness alongside the one he helped kill.

basic.context: Rescued from the mob, Paul asks to speak and, from the barracks steps, tells the crowd his own story in their own language. He was a strict, zealous Pharisee who hunted down Christians until the risen Jesus stopped him on the Damascus road. Ananias restored his sight and named his calling: to be a witness of the Righteous One. In the temple the Lord sent him far away to the Gentiles, and at that word the crowd erupts. Only Paul's Roman citizenship saves him from a flogging.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a testimony inside a narrative, the first of Paul's three tellings of his conversion in Acts. Read it as Paul's chosen defense: not clever argument but the plain account of what Christ did to him. Notice what enrages the crowd, the single word Gentiles, which exposes the real offense of the gospel to those who guarded their privilege as God's people.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul offers an apologia, a reasoned defense, but its content is his testimony. He once persecuted the hodos, the Way. Ananias tells him he will see the dikaios, the Righteous One, and become His martys, His witness, the same word that marks Stephen, whose death Paul had approved. The persecutor becomes the witness of the one he opposed.
basic.typology: Paul's conversion is a pattern of grace: the chief opponent seized and remade by mercy. It anticipates the reach of that mercy to the nations, for the God who could turn a persecutor into a witness can turn the whole Gentile world. The Righteous One Paul sees is the one Israel's own trials had condemned.
basic.christ: The risen Jesus stands at the center. He speaks from heaven, identifies with His persecuted people, and calls Himself Jesus of Nazareth, alive and reigning. He is the Righteous One, the Lord on whose name Paul is baptized and whose witness he becomes. The whole defense is really a proclamation that Jesus is risen and Lord.
basic.god: The God of our fathers, Paul insists, is the very God who appointed him to this calling; the gospel is not a break from Israel's God but His purpose unfolding. God directs each step, from the road to Ananias to the temple vision to the sending to the Gentiles, and even the Roman law that spares Paul serves His design.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 9 and Acts 26 give the other two accounts of Paul's conversion. Acts 7:52 calls Jesus the Righteous One, the title Stephen used. Galatians 1:13-16 is Paul's own summary of his change. Isaiah 49:6 promises a light to the Gentiles, the mission the crowd cannot bear.
basic.oneStory: The book's engine is the gospel going from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth, and this defense shows why: the risen Christ arrested His fiercest enemy and sent him to the nations. The word that inflames the crowd, Gentiles, is the very heart of God's ancient promise, now breaking out through a converted persecutor.

context.literary:
Acts tells the story of Paul's conversion three times (chapters 9, 22 and 26), and each version is shaped for its setting. Chapter 9 is Luke's own narration. Chapter 22 is addressed to a Jerusalem crowd in their own language, and chapter 26 to a Roman governor and a Jewish king. Placing them side by side shows Luke's method. He lets the same events be told with different emphases, so that the reader can see that the core never changes while the presentation does. Here, for instance, Ananias is introduced as a man devout by the law and well spoken of by all the Jews of Damascus, a description chosen to win the crowd, while Acts 26 leaves Ananias out entirely and has the Lord Himself speak the whole commission.

The speech has a clear shape. It opens with a courteous address and an appeal to the audience's own tongue (22:1-2). It moves through Paul's credentials (22:3-5), the Damascus road (22:6-11), Ananias and the commission (22:12-16), the temple vision (22:17-21), and then is cut off by the crowd (22:22). Everything leads to the final word, Gentiles. The speech is built as an ascent toward the single sentence the audience will not tolerate. The first half works to establish that Paul is one of them, and the second reveals that the God of their fathers has sent him outside their borders.

The second half of the chapter, 22:22-30, is a scene of its own, played in the barracks. It mirrors the opening of the chapter by moving from shouting and violence to calm legal procedure, and from the chains of the previous chapter, in which Paul was bound, to the commander's fear at the discovery that he has bound a Roman citizen. The scene ends where the next chapter begins, with Paul standing before the Council.
context.historical:
Paul speaks from the steps of the barracks, the Roman fortress beside the temple court, to a crowd that has just tried to kill him. The language he uses is called Hebrew in the text, and the BSB footnote notes that it may be Aramaic, the common speech of Jews in Palestine. That a Jew from Tarsus can address them in it is itself an argument: he is not a stranger to their world. The crowd falls quieter still when they hear it.

Paul's three verbs in verse 3 are carefully chosen. He was born in Tarsus, raised in Jerusalem, and educated at the feet of Gamaliel. Gamaliel was a Pharisee and a teacher of the law whom all the people honoured, and Luke already introduced him in Acts 5:34 as the voice of moderation in the Sanhedrin. To sit at his feet was the posture of a student, and Paul's mention of it makes him a product of the best the crowd could name. His zeal for the law, he says, was as great as theirs. When he says that he persecuted this Way to the death, he is describing something many of them would have approved. Philippians 3:4-6 gives his own summary of the same credentials, and Galatians 1:13-14 describes his zeal.

The road to Damascus was the route of a man with a commission from the high priest and the council, which together could demand the cooperation of the synagogues there. Damascus had a Jewish community large enough to be worth the journey. Ananias is described as a devout observer of the law, which would reassure a Jewish audience.

The ending of the chapter turns on Roman law. Scourging a Roman citizen who had not been tried and condemned was forbidden, and Paul had used the same protection at Philippi, Acts 16:37. The commander's remark that he paid a high price for his citizenship points to the fact that citizenship could be bought, and Paul's reply that he was born a citizen shows that his family had held the status for at least a generation. His protection was not only a legal tool; it was a form of rank the commander could not match.
context.canonical:
The speech takes up the conversion account first told in Acts 9 and told again in Acts 26. Paul himself adds to it in his letters. Galatians 1:13-17 describes his former life and the way God was pleased to reveal His Son in him. 1 Corinthians 15:8-10 speaks of Christ appearing to him last of all, as to one untimely born, and of the grace that made him what he is. 1 Timothy 1:13-16 says that he was shown mercy as the worst of sinners, so that Christ might display His perfect patience as an example to those who would believe. The Damascus road is the hinge of all of these.

The title the Lord gives Paul's calling reaches back into the Old Testament. In Galatians 1:15, Paul speaks of God setting him apart from his mother's womb, in words that echo Jeremiah 1:5 and the servant of Isaiah 49:1. Isaiah 49:6, where the servant is made a light for the nations to bring salvation to the ends of the earth, is applied to Paul and Barnabas in Acts 13:47. The word the crowd cannot hear, Gentiles, is therefore not a Pauline novelty. It is the promise God made to Abraham and repeated through the prophets.

The speech also takes up Stephen's story. The title 'the Righteous One' was used by Stephen in Acts 7:52, and Paul's mention in 22:20 of standing by while Stephen's blood was shed, and watching over the garments, goes back to Acts 7:58 and 8:1. The first martyr's last prayer, that the Lord not hold the sin against his killers, is answered in the person of the young man at whose feet the cloaks were laid. In Paul's mouth the story of the first martyr becomes the first fruit of the martyr's prayer.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke places this speech where it is for two reasons. The first is apologetic. He wants the reader to see that Paul is not an enemy of the Jewish people but a man who was once as zealous as any of them, who was stopped by the risen Christ, and who has since done nothing except obey a heavenly commission. The testimony makes the case that the gospel is continuous with the faith of Israel: it is the God of our fathers who appointed him, the Righteous One whom he sees, and the call that sends him out.

The second reason concerns the offence of the gospel. The crowd listens until the word Gentiles is spoken, and then it erupts. Luke wants his readers to understand that the real stumbling block was never Paul's conduct. It was the scandal that God would send a message of mercy beyond the people who thought of it as theirs. The point is made by showing how reasonably Paul has argued up to that moment.

There is also a model of witness. Paul does not offer a theological argument. He tells a story: what he was, what happened, what Christ said, what he did. The story is chosen with care for the hearers, but it is true to the facts and returns to the same centre. Luke teaches his readers that the most effective defence of the gospel is often a plain account of what Christ has done, and that a person who tells such a story must be ready for both a hush and a riot.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: Luke records what Paul said and what the crowd did. He does not command believers to repeat the Damascus experience, to expect a heavenly light, or to appeal to their citizenship when in danger. Paul's trance in the temple and the voice of the Lord are descriptions of a unique call to a unique apostle, one of those who, in his own words, had seen Jesus our Lord, 1 Corinthians 9:1. The use of Roman citizenship is likewise something Paul did in his situation, not a rule.\n\nWhat does carry forward is the shape of the testimony: honest about the past, clear about what Christ has done, and unashamed of the people to whom He sends us. Ananias's words in verse 16, 'Get up, be baptized, and wash your sins away, calling on His name', are addressed to Paul but they set out a pattern for the response to the gospel that Acts shows elsewhere, as in 2:38 and 2:21. Believers can also take from the passage the principle that God's patience reaches even the person who is persecuting His people, and that anyone who thinks he is beyond reach should look at Saul. The right use of the law and of citizenship is another lesson: Paul does not resort to his rights to escape the cost of witness, but uses them to keep the road to testimony open.

debates.question: Did Paul's companions hear the voice or not, given Acts 9:7 and Acts 22:9?

views.label: They heard a sound but did not understand the words
views.case: Acts 9:7 says they heard the voice, while 22:9 says they did not understand it. The Greek verb for hear can mean simply perceive a sound or grasp its meaning. The strongest case is that the companions heard a sound but did not comprehend the message addressed to Paul, so the two accounts agree.

views.label: The accounts describe different aspects without contradiction by grammar
views.case: Others resolve it by the object of the verb, noting a shift in case that distinguishes hearing a voice from hearing its content. In 9:7 the noun voice is in the genitive and in 22:9 it is in the accusative. Some scholars caution that this distinction in Greek is not rigid enough to bear the whole weight. The strongest case is that both texts affirm the reality of the encounter while distinguishing Paul's personal reception of the words from the companions' bare perception.

debates.bearing: Either way the point stands: the encounter was real and public enough to leave witnesses, yet the call was Paul's own; Scripture's two accounts complement rather than contradict, and the risen Christ truly spoke.

debates.question: Does 'wash your sins away' in verse 16 teach that baptism forgives sin?

views.label: Baptism is the moment and means by which sins are washed away
views.case: The command is to be baptized and wash away sins, and the two imperatives are joined. Many in the church from early times have taken baptism as the point at which forgiveness is given, as in Acts 2:38, and read Titus 3:5, the washing of new birth, in the same way. The strongest case is the plain sequence of the sentence and the way Acts links baptism with forgiveness.

views.label: Baptism is the outward sign of a washing that God does by grace through faith
views.case: Others point out that the cleansing is attached to calling on His name, which is the act of faith in Joel 2:32 and Romans 10:13, and that the same verbs are in the middle voice, which suggests that Paul is being told to have himself baptized and to have his sins washed, as a visible calling on the Lord. Peter says baptism saves as the pledge of a clear conscience toward God through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, 1 Peter 3:21, not by removing dirt from the body. The strongest case is that Acts elsewhere shows forgiveness and the Spirit coming with faith, as with Cornelius, before baptism, Acts 10:44-48.

debates.bearing: The two views agree that baptism is not optional and that cleansing comes through the Lord Jesus whose name is called upon. They differ on whether the water carries the grace or signs it. Whichever view one holds, the verse forbids delay: Ananias asks Paul what he is waiting for.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 3 holds three participles in a deliberate sequence. Paul says he was gegennemenos, born in Tarsus, anatethrammenos, brought up in Jerusalem, and pepaideumenos, educated at the feet of Gamaliel. The middle verb is a word for nurture, as of a child raised at home. The sequence moves from his origin to his upbringing to his formal teaching, and the claim that he was educated 'in strict conformity' to the law uses akribeia, accuracy or exactness. The same root appears in the Greek of Acts 18:25-26, where Apollos taught accurately and Priscilla and Aquila taught him more accurately, and in 26:5, where Paul calls the Pharisees the strictest party. In this speech Paul is saying that he held the faith of Israel in its most exact form.

The voice from heaven calls 'Saul, Saul', which in the Greek of Acts is the Hebrew form of the name, Saoul, and not the Greek Saulos Luke uses in narration. Jesus addresses him in his native tongue. The question that follows, 'why do you persecute Me?', makes no distinction between the Lord and His people: to attack the church is to attack Him. When Paul asks 'Who are You, Lord?' the word kyrie may mean no more than sir, but the answer, 'Jesus of Nazareth', shows that Paul is already beginning to speak of the Lord in the larger sense.

The contested point is the hearing of the voice. Acts 9:7 says the companions heard the voice using the genitive case, while 22:9 says they did not hear it using the accusative. A traditional rule says that the genitive means hearing a sound and the accusative means hearing with understanding, which would reconcile the passages. The rule is not as firm in Greek as it sounds, and careful readers do not rest the whole case on it, but it shows that the two verses use different constructions and therefore need not conflict. Acts 26:14 adds that all fell to the ground, where Acts 9:7 says they stood speechless, and the likely explanation is that they fell first and then rose.

Ananias tells Paul in verse 14 that God has 'appointed' him, using procheirizo, to choose in advance or to hand-pick. Luke uses the same verb of the Christ appointed for the people in Acts 3:20 and in the commission in Acts 26:16, so Paul's call is described in the vocabulary used of Christ's own appointment. The title 'the Righteous One' is ton dikaion, a title Acts uses elsewhere of Jesus, Acts 3:14 and 7:52. The phrase 'to hear His voice' is literally to hear a voice from His mouth, which is how Paul came to count himself among those who had seen the Lord.

In verse 16 both imperatives, baptisai and apolousai, are in the middle voice, and the participle 'calling on' is epikalesamenos, also middle. The middle voice suggests that Paul is to have himself baptized and to have his sins washed away as acts in which he is personally involved. The phrase 'calling on His name' uses the language of Joel 2:32, which Peter had quoted in Acts 2:21 as a promise to be fulfilled in Jesus. To call on the name of the Lord in the Old Testament was to call on God Himself, and Ananias uses the phrase of Jesus.

Finally, in verse 21 God says 'I will send you far away', using exapostello, a compound of the verb from which apostle comes. Paul's call is a commissioning, and its direction is makran, far off, the same word Peter used in Acts 2:39 for those who are far off.

typology.type: The servant called from the womb, Acts 22:14-15 and Galatians 1:15
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 49:1 has the Servant say that the LORD called Him from the womb, and Jeremiah 1:5 has the prophet set apart before birth to be a prophet to the nations. Paul describes his own call in those terms in Galatians 1:15-16, and Ananias's words here, that God appointed him to know His will and be His witness to everyone, take up the same pattern. The escalation is that the call to the nations, which Isaiah placed on the Servant, now travels through an apostle. The type falls short because Paul is a participant in the Servant's mission, not the Servant. The light for the nations is first of all Christ, and Paul is the lamp that carries it.

Isaiah 53:11 speaks of the Lord's righteous Servant who will justify many and bear their iniquities. Stephen called Jesus the Righteous One in Acts 7:52, and Peter used the title in Acts 3:14. Paul's seeing the Righteous One in the road marks him as a witness of the risen Lord, in the company of those who had seen Him, 1 Corinthians 9:1. The escalation is that the suffering Servant of Isaiah is now vindicated and living, speaking from heaven. The correspondence falls short in only one way: the title in Isaiah is a promise, and in Acts it is a person who can be seen, heard and obeyed, so the type is fully met.

typology.type: Stephen's blood and the garments at Paul's feet, Acts 22:20
typology.fulfillment: The garment-keeper at Stephen's stoning, Acts 7:58, becomes the witness who speaks of him with reverence, calling him 'Your witness'. The correspondence is not a type in the strict sense but a pattern of the way God answers the prayer of a dying servant. Stephen prayed that the Lord not hold this sin against his killers, Acts 7:60, and the answer is in the speaker. The escalation is in Christ, who prayed 'Father, forgive them' for His own killers. The pattern falls short in that Stephen's prayer was for forgiveness and Paul's conversion was the grace of God in action, not a reward for Stephen's prayer.

typology.type: Washed by calling on His name, Acts 22:16
typology.fulfillment: Ezekiel 36:25-27 promised that God would sprinkle clean water on His people, cleanse them from all impurities and idols, and give them a new heart and His Spirit. Ananias's call to be baptized and wash away sins by calling on the Lord's name sets this promise in a personal commission. The escalation is that the washing is attached to Jesus. Paul later writes that believers were washed, sanctified and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit, 1 Corinthians 6:11. The type falls short only in its form: Ezekiel promised cleansing without saying how, and Acts says how, through faith in the one whose name is called on, in a washing that the Spirit applies.

study.christ:
The Damascus road account shows Christ in four ways. First, He is alive. The man who set out to hunt down the followers of a dead teacher meets Jesus of Nazareth speaking from heaven. The resurrection is not argued in this speech. It is presupposed in every line, because a dead man does not speak, and the one who does speak says 'I am Jesus of Nazareth'. The Jesus who was crucified under a Roman governor has been raised, exalted and given a voice that knocks a man to the ground. Acts 26:23 gives Paul's own summary: the Christ would suffer, and as the first to rise from the dead would proclaim light to the people and the Gentiles.

Second, Christ identifies with His people. 'Why do you persecute Me?' is a question about the church, and it shows that the union between the Lord and His followers is so close that blows against them land on Him. This is the root of the teaching Paul will develop about the church as the body of Christ. Jesus had already taught the same thing in Matthew 25:40, and John 15:18-21 had said that persecution of the disciples comes because of His name. On the road, the Lord Himself says it to the persecutor.

Third, Christ is the Righteous One. The title carries the weight of the Old Testament's promised servant, Isaiah 53:11, and the memory of Stephen's accusation that Israel had killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One, Acts 7:52. By using it in front of a hostile Jerusalem crowd, Paul is saying that the man their rulers condemned is the one the prophets foretold, and that he has seen Him.

Fourth, Christ is the one whose name is called on for washing. The phrase borrowed from Joel 2:32 applies to the LORD, and Ananias applies it to Jesus. To call on His name is to treat Him as the God who saves. Romans 10:12-13 draws the conclusion in so many words: the same Lord is Lord of all, and everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. The one who stopped Saul on the road is the Lord of Joel's promise.

The chapter should not be pressed into forced allegory. The noon light is not a code for anything, and the scales that fell from the eyes in Acts 9:18 are not mentioned here. What the text gives is simpler and larger: Jesus is risen, He speaks, He owns His people, He is the Righteous One, and He sends His witness to the nations, which is exactly what the crowd cannot bear to hear.
study.god:
This chapter shows God as the one who takes the initiative. Paul does not seek Christ. He is on his way to arrest Christ's people when light flashes around him. In verse 14 Ananias says that the God of our fathers has appointed him, and the verbs that follow, to know His will, to see the Righteous One, to hear His voice, all have God as the subject. The same pattern holds in the temple vision: Paul prays and the Lord appears and gives the instruction. Even when he argues, protesting that the people in Jerusalem know how he persecuted believers, the Lord does not debate but sends. Grace here is not a reward for effort but an intervention.

The chapter also shows God's faithfulness to what He has already said. Paul insists that the God of our fathers is the one who has called him. The mission to the Gentiles is not a new god's project; it is the carrying out of the promise made to Abraham and sung by Isaiah. The tension is that the very people who are meant to rejoice in the promise are the ones who rise up against its fulfilment. God holds together His commitment to Israel and His purpose for the nations, and He does so by sending a Jew, trained at Jerusalem, to speak in Hebrew to his own people about a light for the world.

There is a lesson in the way God uses ordinary means in the chapter. He sends Ananias, a devout and respected man, to lay hands on a former enemy, and tells him what to say. He lets a Roman commander's fear and a Roman statute keep Paul from a scourging. The same God who speaks from heaven also works through law and procedure, and Paul uses the means with a good conscience. Romans 13:1 would later say that governing authorities have been appointed by God, and the chapter shows how that works in practice.

The doctrine of God that emerges is of a God who is patient with His enemies. 1 Timothy 1:16 says that Paul was shown mercy so that Christ might display His perfect patience as an example. The same Lord who stopped the persecutor is the one who sends him, and the sending is itself part of the mercy.

For worship, the speech invites two responses. One is wonder at a God who chooses, who finds the person least likely to turn and turns him. The other is willingness to be sent. Paul's own protest in the temple, that surely his past makes him the wrong choice for Jerusalem, is answered with a single word, 'Go!', and the whole of his later life shows what worship looks like when it obeys that word.

crossReferences.note: The first account of the Damascus road, told by Luke in his own voice. Reading it beside Acts 22 shows what Paul chooses to emphasise for the crowd, such as Ananias's reputation for keeping the law, and what stays constant: the light, the voice, the blindness, the healing and the baptism.

Stephen says Israel killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One and has now become His betrayer and murderer. Paul uses the same title in Acts 22:14, and he does so in front of a Jerusalem crowd. The title ties Paul's call to the first martyr's witness.

Paul's own summary of what he was and how God was pleased to reveal His Son in him so that he might preach Him among the Gentiles. It confirms the speech from his own pen and uses the language of being set apart from the womb, which echoes Isaiah and Jeremiah.

The Servant is made a light for the nations so that God's salvation may reach the ends of the earth. It is the promise behind the word that the crowd cannot bear. Paul and Barnabas apply it to their own work in Acts 13:47, and Paul tells Agrippa that the Christ would proclaim light to the Gentiles, Acts 26:23.

Paul's third telling of the Damascus road, before Agrippa. It records that all fell to the ground and that the Lord spoke in Hebrew, and it places the whole commission in the Lord's own mouth. Together with Acts 9 and 22 it gives three angles on a single event, each adding detail without contradicting the others.

The witnesses laid their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul. Paul's memory in 22:20 that he stood by approving and watching over the garments takes the reader back to this scene. The speech does not hide the worst thing in his past but turns it into the reason for his certainty that grace is real.

Paul says he was a blasphemer, a persecutor and a violent man, yet was shown mercy so that Christ might display His perfect patience as an example to those who would believe. It reads like a commentary on the speech, explaining why he tells the story at all.

Everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved. Ananias's command to wash away sins by calling on His name uses this language of the Lord Jesus. The echo is part of the New Testament's claim that the name belonging to the God of Israel is rightly given to Jesus.

At Philippi Paul and Silas use their Roman citizenship after being beaten without trial. In Acts 22:25 Paul uses it earlier, before the flogging begins. Reading the two scenes together shows that he treats citizenship as a tool to protect his witness and as something to be used with care.

Paul says Christ appeared to him last of all, as to one untimely born, and that he is the least of the apostles because he persecuted the church of God. But by God's grace he is what he is. It states in a sentence the experience that Acts 22 narrates, and it shows how personally he took it.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story is the story of a promise to bless all nations and of the repeated failure of God's people to keep up with it. God told Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, Genesis 12:3. Israel was meant to be a kingdom of priests for the world, but it kept the blessing as its own possession. The prophets kept returning to the point: Isaiah's Servant would be a light for the nations, and Jonah, the reluctant prophet, was sent to a Gentile city and was angry that it repented. The crowd outside the temple is the same impulse in a later generation. They hear a testimony that has taken them to the edge of the promise and then they cannot bear the final word.

The chapter also answers the question of what God does with His enemies. The story from Genesis onward is full of rebels, from Cain to Pharaoh to the kings of Israel, and the Bible does not minimise their guilt. Here is a persecutor who is stopped, not destroyed. Saul is struck blind and sent into Damascus to wait, and what is waiting for him is a disciple with words of welcome. God's answer to His enemy's rage is to make him an ambassador. If this is how the Lord deals with the worst of His opponents, no one is outside the reach of the story.

The speech also marks a turn in the book of Acts. The word of the Lord began in Jerusalem, spread to Judea and Samaria, and has been advancing among the Gentiles. In Paul's testimony the advance is traced to its source, and the crowd's reaction explains why the message goes the way it does. From here Paul is a prisoner. He will stand before the Council, governors and a king, and the road ends in Rome. The same Lord who said 'Go! I will send you far away' will say to Paul in the barracks that he must testify in Rome.

The end of the story is already visible in the speech. The Gentiles whose mention caused a riot are the nations that Revelation sees standing before the throne, drawn from every tribe, language and people. The crowd's cry in Jerusalem, 'Rid the earth of him', is answered in the new creation by a multitude from every nation praising the Lamb. The persecutor became a witness so that every nation might become worshippers.

quiz.q: How does Paul choose to defend himself before the crowd?

options.text: By telling the story of how the risen Christ met and changed him.
options.note: Paul's defense is testimony: his conversion and commission are the argument.

options.text: By reciting his Jewish credentials and training under Gamaliel.
options.note: He does open with these, but they serve to lead into the testimony that is his real defense.

options.text: By quoting Roman law to prove his innocence.
options.note: He invokes his citizenship later to stop a flogging, but his defense to the crowd is his testimony, not legal argument.

options.text: By denying that he had ever persecuted the church.
options.note: The opposite: he openly confesses that he persecuted the Way to the death.

quiz.q: What single word turned the crowd from silence to fury?

options.text: Gentiles, when Paul said the Lord sent him far away to them.
options.note: The crowd listened until that word, then shouted for his death.

options.text: His claim to have seen and heard the risen Jesus.
options.note: This was provocative, but the text marks the sending to the Gentiles as the breaking point.

options.text: His mention of Stephen's death.
options.note: He recalls Stephen, but the crowd's eruption comes at the word Gentiles, not there.

options.text: His claim to be a Roman citizen.
options.note: That claim comes afterward, to the officers, and it quiets the flogging rather than inflaming the crowd.

quiz.q: Who did the voice from heaven say He was, and what does it reveal?

options.text: Jesus of Nazareth, alive and so united to His people that persecuting them is persecuting Him.
options.note: The risen Christ names Himself and identifies with those Paul was hunting.

options.text: The Lord who was calling Paul to a new mission.
options.note: True, but it omits the striking self-identification with the persecuted church that the words reveal.

options.text: An angel sent to redirect Paul's zeal.
options.note: It was not an angel but the risen Jesus Himself who spoke.

options.text: The God of the Gentiles, unknown to Israel.
options.note: He is Jesus of Nazareth, and Paul insists this is the God of the fathers, not a foreign deity.

quiz.q: How did Paul's Roman citizenship matter in this scene?

options.text: It made it unlawful to flog him without a trial, so the soldiers drew back.
options.note: Paul's citizenship halted the scourging and alarmed the commander.

options.text: It gained him a respectful hearing from the commander.
options.note: It did change how the commander treated him, but its specific effect here was to stop the flogging.

options.text: It proved to the crowd that he was innocent.
options.note: The crowd was not persuaded by it; the citizenship affected the Romans, not the mob.

options.text: It required him to be executed under Roman law.
options.note: The reverse: it protected him from unlawful punishment.

quiz.q: What did Ananias say God had appointed Paul to be?

options.text: A witness to everyone of what he had seen and heard of the Righteous One.
options.note: Ananias names the calling: to see the Righteous One and be His witness to all.

options.text: A teacher of the law to the Jews in Damascus.
options.note: Paul did reason with Jews, but the appointment named was to be Christ's witness to everyone.

options.text: A judge over the churches he had once persecuted.
options.note: Nothing here appoints Paul as a judge; he is appointed a witness.

options.text: A priest to serve in the temple.
options.note: No priestly office is given; his calling is to witness to the risen Christ.

questions: Paul's whole defense was simply the story of what Jesus did to him. How ready are you to tell your own story of Christ's work in your life?
The risen Jesus said, why do you persecute Me, treating harm to His people as harm to Himself. How does it change your view of the church to know Christ takes it that personally?
One word, Gentiles, exposed the crowd's real offense. Where might you be quietly resisting the truth that God's grace is for people unlike you?
Paul, who had approved a witness's death, was made a witness himself. What does his story tell you about whom God's mercy can reach and remake?
Ananias told Paul to get up, be baptized, and wash his sins away, calling on Christ's name. What is God calling you to stop waiting on and do?
God used even Roman law to protect His servant for the work ahead. Where can you trust that God is ordering the ordinary circumstances of your life for His purposes?

translationNotes.note: In Hebrew carries a footnoted alternative, in Aramaic; literally in the Hebrew language, naming the local tongue that quieted the crowd.

The companions saw the light but could not understand the voice; compare Acts 9:7. The Greek verb for hear can mean perceive a sound or grasp its meaning, so the accounts agree: they heard a sound but did not comprehend the words.
Your witness Stephen carries a footnoted alternative, martyr; the same Greek word underlies both, and it links Paul's new calling as witness to the death he once approved.
